Microsoft unveiled its Maia 300 AI chip this month and says it delivers 40% more output per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems. Production starts early next year. If Azure grows 44% to 45% or faster and Microsoft shows Copilot use deepening, the rally has support. If Azure lands on guidance but capital spending rises faster than cash flow and Microsoft gives no new Copilot data, the stock could stall, since expectations have moved up. If Azure growth falls short, capacity limits persist or OpenAI news hits the backlog, the AI-spending worry that sent shares down after the fiscal 2026 third-quarter report could return. title: What Did It Take To Hold Microsoft Stock? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. Over the last ten years, Microsoft (MSFT) stock turned $10,000 into $92,451 before dividends. That same $10,000 invested in the S&P 500 became $35,968. Looking back makes the strategy seem as simple as buying and waiting, but holding the shares required far more discipline. How many times do you think Microsoft stock fell 20% or more along the way? Microsoft stock fell 20% or more from a closing high four times. Two of those declines exceeded 30%. All four are listed below. Falls of 20% or more from a closing high, Oct 2016 to Oct 2026. Split-adjusted closing prices, dividends excluded. The deepest drop occurred between November 2021 and November 2022, when the stock fell 37.6% while the S&P 500 lost 20.8%. Investors spent about 19 months below the previous peak until the shares closed above that old high in June 2023. The real question was never just whether to buy Microsoft. It was whether you could sit through falls like these. What Did Holding Microsoft Through A Fall Feel Like? The most recent decline began at a closing high on October 28, 2025, and the stock took nearly eight months to reach its low on June 25, 2026, dropping 34.9%. The S&P 500 rose 6.8% over those same months, so shareholders lost ground while the broader market gained. From that low, the stock took another 3.6 months to close above its old high. All four of Microsoft’s declines eventually ended. Nobody holding shares in the middle of a drop knew that at the time, however, and an investor in the spring of 2026 had no way to know this one would. Microsoft generates revenue from cloud services such as Azure and software such as Microsoft 365. Its two largest segments are Intelligent Cloud, followed by Productivity and Business Processes. During the deepest fall, revenue over twelve months rose 15.2%, and the operating margin stayed close to 42% from the high to the low. In the latest fall, which was shorter, twelve-month revenue rose 8.3% from the high to the low, and the operating margin edged up from 46.3% to 46.8%. Sales grew and operating margins held steady during both falls while the stock declined. A drop like that, while the business keeps growing, is the risk of holding the shares. Microsoft stock is up 148.2% since its November 2022 low, and anyone who sold there missed all of it. Today, the stock sits 2.1% below the high it set on October 13, 2026. Enduring those four falls was the cost of the ten-year gain, and the investors who captured those returns were the ones who sat through every drop. Microsoft’s revenue kept growing during both the deepest decline and the latest one. The next time Microsoft stock falls hard, check whether its revenue is falling with it. Not necessarily on Microsoft alone, if your goal is long-term wealth. Wealth is built by owning the companies that keep outperforming, the leaders of their industries, wherever they are. Here are two companies from Microsoft’s own industry that have beaten it. Over the five years to October 2026, Fortinet stock rose 156% and CommVault Systems stock rose 105%, while Microsoft stock rose 80%. title: Trump’s Data Center ‘Dividend’ Proposal Puts MSFT, AMZN, GOOGL, META In Focus - Stocktwits
content: President Donald Trump on Wednesday urged companies building artificial intelligence (AI) data centers to pay local communities or individual residents a “dividend” to secure support for new projects. In a Truth Social post, Trump said previously unpopular projects had gained support after companies reached financial agreements with communities. “MAKE DEALS, and get them built!!!” Trump wrote. Trump also said large new data centers must generate their own electricity and supply or sell excess power to the grid, potentially lowering electricity costs. He did not specify how the dividend payments would work. Rapid AI infrastructure expansion has become a political flashpoint as communities question how energy-intensive facilities affect electricity bills, water supplies, and local infrastructure. The U.S. Department of Energy estimated that data centers could account for 6.7% to 12% of national electricity consumption by 2028, compared with 4.4% in 2023. A July report from Carbon Direct found that community opposition had delayed, withdrawn, or stalled at least 46 projects across 20 states, representing $170 billion in announced investments. In a recent TIME interview, Trump acknowledged concerns about data centers being built near homes. “It doesn't mean I want them right next to my house, but certainly I like them in my county,” he said. The president also argued that the facilities would bring economic benefits, saying, “They're going to lower your taxes.” At an October 3 rally in Ohio, he defended data-center development, warning that investments could shift to China if the U.S. blocked projects. In March, Amazon, Google (GOOG, GOOGL), Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle (ORCL) and xAI signed the White House's Ratepayer Protection Pledge, agreeing to cover additional power generation and infrastructure costs associated with their facilities. Trump’s proposal to pay local communities a dividend for hosting AI data centers is “not crazy to consider,” according to Nebius Group N.V. (NBIS) Chief Revenue Officer Marc Boroditsky, who told CNBC that the company was “100% in principle” open to discussions about investing in local communities. Boroditsky said community benefits could extend beyond existing tax revenues to education, job development and direct economic opportunities. Investor Shay Boloor, in an X post, highlighted that the proposal could favor technology giants such as Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL), Amazon (AMZN), Microsoft (MSFT) and Meta (META). Boloor said paying residents and developing on-site power generation could prove far cheaper for these companies than delaying billions of dollars in AI infrastructure investments for another year. GE Aerospace (GE) CEO Larry Culp said demand remains “solid” across the business despite a dynamic operating environment, as the company delivered double-digit revenue growth and stronger profits in the third quarter (Q3). Retail sentiment reflected optimism around engine demand, rising deliveries and efforts to expand production capacity. GE Aerospace stock edged 1% higher in Wednesday’s premarket. The stock fell 3.6% on Tuesday to its worst day in two months. During the Q3 earnings call, Culp said GE Aerospace is expanding production and developing new technologies to meet customer needs. “Demand continues to be solid across the business even in a dynamic environment,” said Culp. He added that GE Aerospace's total revenue rose 18% from last year, while operating profit increased 30%. The company recorded an operating margin of 22.5%, an improvement of 220 basis points, and earnings per share climbed 36%. Free cash flow exceeded $2 billion during the quarter. “These results reflect the impact of FLIGHT DECK fundamentals to drive continued output momentum with year-to-date commercial services revenue and total engine deliveries both up over 20%.” Culp said GE Aerospace is using its FLIGHT DECK operating system to improve safety, quality, delivery performance and costs and added that this approach helped its workforce reorganize the LEAP fan assembly production line and establish standardized procedures across workstations. These changes enabled the team to more than double output, expanding capacity to support growth in the LEAP engine fleet. According to reports, Microsoft plans to launch an Xbox handheld device during the 2027 holiday season and introduce the next-generation Xbox console, codenamed "Project Helix," in the 2028 holiday season. Zhitong Finance APP has learned that Microsoft (MSFT.US) is accelerating its rollout of the next-generation gaming hardware lineup. According to reports, Microsoft plans to launch an Xbox handheld device during the 2027 holiday season and introduce the next-generation Xbox console, codenamed "Project Helix," in the 2028 holiday season. According to reports, the new gaming console codenamed "Project Helix" will leverage AMD's (AMD.US) FSR 4.1 machine-learning technology. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma described Project Helix as "a family of devices," suggesting that Microsoft's future hardware ecosystem will no longer be confined to a single form factor. Coupled with the multi-year strategic partnership Microsoft and AMD struck last year, this lineup of devices is highly likely to be built on AMD's latest chips. The report also indicates that, absent hardware subsidies, the next-generation console could retail for as much as $1,200 to $1,800. At the software development level, Microsoft's internal Windows team and Xbox team once clashed over control of the next-generation device's operating system. Given that the two sides have experienced similar friction numerous times over the past 25 years, this conflict was hardly surprising. However, current reports indicate that the Xbox team has regained control of the software direction for Project Helix. In addition, Xbox's core subscription service, Game Pass, is also undergoing major adjustments. Reports indicate that Microsoft is drawing on Netflix's model to revamp Game Pass's tiered structure, planning to introduce multiple options—some with ads and others without—and considering the addition of premium service packages for console exclusives, cloud gaming, and multiplayer modes. This move will enhance the service's flexibility, though it remains unclear whether first‑day blockbusters will be included in the subscription or how overall pricing will change. One of Shal's first moves after taking office was to overhaul Game Pass's pricing strategy. She acknowledged internally that "Game Pass was too expensive for players." Subsequently, Microsoft not only lowered subscription prices but also stripped new Call of Duty titles of their exclusive launch status on Game Pass. In addition, Shalma plans to initiate a new round of Xbox layoffs this month, with further cuts scheduled for November and January. Under Sharma's leadership, the Xbox management team has been working to improve the division's operations and accelerate its growth. The division employs roughly 14,000 people but has struggled in recent years with extremely low profit margins and declining sales. In the fiscal year ending in June, Xbox revenue fell 7% to $21.8 billion. According to Microsoft's disclosure earlier this year, the division's "accountable margin" (similar to adjusted profit margin) has continued to decline over the past year, dropping to just 3% as of June. Previously, Microsoft had hoped to generate substantial new revenue by acquiring numerous game studios, but the results fell short of expectations. Since taking over the division in February this year, Sharma has been working to reverse its declining performance. According to reports, she unveiled a plan in July to cut 3,200 jobs—about 20% of the workforce—over the next year, while ramping up investment in game franchises such as Halo and Minecraft. Notably, according to insiders, several private equity firms have been exploring the possibility of acquiring Microsoft's Xbox gaming business in recent months. If such a deal were to materialize, the business could be valued at between $100 billion and $150 billion. These sources indicated that these discussions among private equity firms are still at an early exploratory stage and have not yet evolved into formal negotiations with Microsoft. Nevertheless, this suggests that if Microsoft struggles to turn around its struggling gaming division, the company could still find a buyer. In response, a Microsoft spokesperson stated in a statement, "Xbox is not for sale," and declined to offer further comment. title: S&P 500 Could Hit 8,000 Soon, Morningstar Says — CRM, NOW, WDAY And MSFT Lead The August Rebound - Stocktwits
content: Software stocks are having a comeback moment. After recent concerns that generative AI could undermine traditional SaaS business models, Salesforce, ServiceNow and Workday are suddenly back in focus as investors look for ways to play AI beyond the chip trade. The rotation has caught Morningstar market strategist’s attention, who believes that the S&P 500 could reach 8,000 within weeks, after rapidly recovering from its July losses. Morningstar Chief U.S. Market Strategist Dave Sekera said recent market action had reversed the traditional pattern of stocks climbing gradually and falling quickly. “What we saw over the course of July, the stock market, where it’s taken the stairs down, here at the beginning of August, really just taking the elevator up,” Sekera said on Morningstar’s The Morning Filter podcast on Monday. The market recovered all its July losses in four trading sessions and reached new highs, he said. With the S&P 500 about 3% below 8,000, Sekera added that he “wouldn’t be surprised” to see it reach that level within the next few weeks. Beneath the index rally, Sekera identified a rotation away from stocks closely related to AI capital spending as investors questioned whether companies would earn sufficient long-term returns on their massive investments. The analyst said investors had rotated out of AI hardware stocks including Sandisk, Micron, Ciena and Western Digital, while beaten-down software names such as Salesforce, ServiceNow, Workday and Microsoft staged strong rebounds. “It’s really interesting seeing what’s going on underneath the surface as opposed to just looking at the headline index level,” he said. Workday became a major catalyst for the software rebound after Silver Lake reportedly entered discussions to acquire the company. The talks had reportedly continued for months, and Silver Lake could recruit co-investors. While no deal is guaranteed, an acquisition could rank among the largest software take-private transactions ever. Morgan Stanley said a transaction would validate Workday’s “strong moat and large opportunity to automate the back-office.” The optimism spread across the sector, lifting Salesforce, Adobe, ServiceNow and SAP following the report. ServiceNow’s second-quarter (Q2) results offered evidence that enterprise software companies can capture AI spending instead of losing business to emerging tools. The company’s AI-related annual contract value crossed $1 billion, while agentic AI deployments in production increased ninefold over nine months. Subscription revenue grew 24% from a year ago, renewal rates reached 98% and ServiceNow raised its full-year subscription-revenue outlook. Investors now view ServiceNow as a potential control layer for enterprise AI agents as its platform holds the historical workflow data and business context needed to deploy them. Salesforce’s Agentforce platform is also gaining traction. Its annual recurring revenue hit $1.2 billion in the first quarter of fiscal 2027, up 205% from the previous year. Combined Agentforce and Data 360 annual recurring revenue reached $3.4 billion. Salesforce also processed 28.6 trillion AI tokens during the quarter, up 152% sequentially, and raised the lower end of its full-year revenue guidance. Microsoft reinforced the software bull case with fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $90 billion, up 18%, and 43% growth in Azure and other cloud services. Azure’s annual revenue surpassed $100 billion for the first time, while Microsoft’s commercial remaining performance obligations jumped 84% to $678 billion. Microsoft 365 Copilot also exceeded 30 million paid seats. Microsoft CFO Amy Hood said sequential backlog growth came largely from commitments outside the biggest U.S. AI model developers, signaling that demand was increasing. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around CRM was ‘bearish’ amid ‘normal’ message volume, while NOW and MSFT were also ‘bearish’ with ‘low’ activity. WDAY stood apart with ‘bullish’ sentiment and ‘high’ message volume. Over the past year, CRM has fallen 16%, NOW 28%, WDAY 14% and MSFT 4%. Nebius on Wednesday raised its debt offering to $5 billion from $4.5 billion. The third debt raise of more than $1 billion in a year, coupled with over $8 billion already on its balance sheet, gives the AI infrastructure company significant financial firepower to accelerate its ongoing expansion. Proceeds from the offering will be used to expand data center capacity, ​invest in the company's full-stack AI cloud ​platform, and acquire GPUs and other key components needed ‌to ⁠support growth, Nebius said on Wednesday. Amid its expansion drive, rumors are swirling that Nebius has entered the race to acquire Israeli AI startup Decart AI. Israeli tech outlet CTech reported that SpaceX, Nvidia and Amazon are also in negotiations for a deal that could be worth $6 billion to $7 billion, following earlier reports that Anthropic is eyeing the company as well. Decart AI builds real-time generative AI models and infrastructure, best known for Oasis, its AI-generated Minecraft-like game, and Mirage, which transforms live video using text prompts. The real prize is the custom Optimization Stack, which can reportedly boost GPU inference throughput by up to eight times on the same hardware – potentially a major advantage for cloud companies. Nebius is a relatively new neocloud player that recently pivoted toward cloud computing and is now building capacity to fulfill its first set of major orders. The Amsterdam, Netherlands-based company signed a five-year, $12 billion AI infrastructure deal with Meta Platforms and is targeting 800 MW to 1 GW of connected power by the end of 2026, with data center campuses across Missouri, Pennsylvania, Finland and the UK. Amid massive demand for AI cloud capacity, neocloud stocks have surged. Nebius is up a staggering 218% year to date, while CoreWeave and IREN have gained 44% and 14%, respectively. Stocktwits recently published an explainer comparing the three neocloud stocks from an investment perspective. Datavault AI (DVLT stock is headed for a weekly loss after a blown-out earnings miss, an $88 million net loss, and a near-24% single-day plunge. Yet retail traders who had piled into the data-tokenization company aren't retreating; they are doubling down, betting that a flurry of acquisitions will turn Wednesday's carnage into a comeback. Datavault’s second-quarter (Q2) results badly missed Wall Street's revenue targets, triggering a roughly 23.4% drop on Wednesday. EPS showed a loss of $0.12 per share, worse than the $0.03 loss analysts expected, according to Fiscal Ai estimates. The company’s net loss also jumped to $88 million, more than twice the $37.1 million loss reported a year earlier. But the sell-off has coincided with an aggressive expansion push, a completed acquisition of exchange operator NYIAX and a new definitive agreement to buy Wyoming-chartered bank BankWyse that retail traders are framing as the missing pieces of a much bigger tokenization platform. Datavault AI stock traded over 1% higher overnight, ahead of Thursday. Datavault AI is doubling down on its ambitious growth plans, with CEO Nathaniel Bradley reaffirming the company’s goal of generating $200 million in revenue during 2026. The comments came as the company expands its data monetization business through tokenization, financial infrastructure, banking and cybersecurity. The company is working with Available Networks, which Bradley said is developing an AI supercompute network spanning more than 100 cities and 1,000 locations. Through Project Qestrel, Datavault AI plans to create a digital token system for Available Networks that would allow the company to measure and manage access to its infrastructure. title: Boeing Teams Up With Microsoft To Build New AI-Powered Dataliner Platform – BMO Sees ‘Upside Tension’ For Azure - TradingView
content: BA shares were in focus on Tuesday after Boeing announced Dataliner, an AI-powered data intelligence platform developed with Microsoft (MSFT) to help airlines improve fleet-wide maintenance and operational decisions. BA and MSFT shares traded marginally lower at the time of writing. Dataliner combines aviation data, AI and Boeing’s aircraft and engineering expertise to give airlines a more complete view of their fleets, including aircraft condition, maintenance history and operations. “Dataliner is an important step in how Boeing is bringing its aircraft expertise and digital capabilities together to help customers anticipate maintenance needs, identify emerging risks and take timely action,” said Lindsey Douglas, vice president of Cabin, Modifications, Maintenance and Digital Services at Boeing Global Services. Developed in partnership with Microsoft, Dataliner uses Azure AI Foundry, Microsoft’s data solutions and other technologies. Dataliner allows airlines to keep data in their own environments and choose what information they share. They can access Boeing and industry intelligence through applications, APIs, analytics and AI-enabled experiences. Boeing said Dataliner includes access controls, encryption and monitoring to help protect sensitive aviation data. Its on-demand sharing model does not require airlines to centralize their data on a single platform. “By combining Boeing’s OEM and aviation expertise with Microsoft’s trusted data and AI technologies, Dataliner gives airlines a secure, scalable foundation to turn fragmented data into fleet-wide intelligence,” said Chris Barry, president of U.S. Public Sector Industries at Microsoft. Dataliner To Support Boeing’s Digital Services Portfolio Boeing also said that Dataliner will provide a common intelligence foundation for its Digital Services portfolio. It will support the development of Asset Lifecycle Planning and TechOps AI Agent, while creating opportunities to bring greater connectivity and intelligence to existing products, including Airplane Health Management, Insight Accelerator and Maintenance Performance Toolbox. Separately, BMO Capital on Tuesday raised its price target on Microsoft to $600 from $515 while maintaining an ‘Outperform’ rating, according to The Fly. The firm sees “upside tension” to its first quarter (Q1) Azure revenue estimates, citing positive cloud-check feedback. BMO also believes Azure revenue can “accelerate in Q1 vs. Q1.” For Microsoft 365, BMO said the company’s shift toward a consumption-based model could support average revenue per user and sales mix as seat growth moderates. title: Microsoft, Alphabet and Goldman Sachs join objections to OKX-ICE tokenized stock trading - CoinDesk
content:
Microsoft MSFT$532.98·Market Closed, Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL) and Goldman Sachs (GS) have objected to having tokenized versions of their shares traded on OKXICE, adding to issuer resistance against the planned stock-trading venue from crypto exchange OKX and New York Stock Exchange parent Intercontinental Exchange (ICE). The companies appear among seven additional objecting issuers in the joint venture’s updated public notice dated Oct. 19. Qualcomm (QCOM), Caterpillar (CAT), McDonald’s (MCD) and Western Digital (WDC) also joined the list. The additions bring the disclosed tally to 16 companies, up from nine in last week’s notice. The document does not explain their reasons or specify when they submitted their objections. Read more: SEC tokenized stock framework faces issuer pushback as Broadcom, Verizon object to OKX-ICE listing The growing list highlights a hurdle for the SEC’s new framework for tokenized stock trading, which was unveiled last month. OKXICE’s original notice identified 63 tickers representing 62 companies, with Alphabet appearing through both share classes. Fifteen of those companies have now objected, leaving 47 without a disclosed objection. Cerebras Systems (CBRS), the other objecting issuer, was outside the original proposed trading roster. Previous objectors also included Broadcom (AVGO), Verizon (VZ), UnitedHealth (UNH), CoreWeave (CRWV), AppLovin (APP), Applied Digital (APLD), Rocket Lab (RKLB) and Applied Optoelectronics (AAOI). OKXICE announced its plans on Oct. 5, seeking to operate under the SEC’s five-year “Innovation Exemption.” The framework allows qualifying venues to trade tokenized U.S. stocks through automated market makers and liquidity pools, while giving issuers an opportunity to object. Microsoft's (MSFT) Azure cloud business is facing fresh scrutiny as the company reportedly considers ways to reduce costs by as much as 20%, even as demand for its cloud and AI services remains strong. According to reports, Azure President Girish Bablani asked senior leaders in his roughly 11,500-person unit to identify potential cost reductions of at least 20%. Microsoft has pushed back on the report, saying Azure leadership has not directed teams to develop cost-cutting plans. The reported cost-cutting discussions come at a time when Microsoft is seeing surging artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure spending that puts pressure on margins. Meanwhile, Microsoft is ramping up its own AI-chip deployments and expects capital expenditures to remain elevated, highlighting the challenge of balancing rapid AI growth with profitability. While a successful reduction in Azure expenses could improve operating leverage and help offset the massive costs of expanding AI capacity, the aggressive cuts could also raise questions about whether Microsoft is sacrificing investment to protect margins. Microsoft Corporation is a global technology company headquartered in Redmond, Washington, with a broad portfolio spanning software, cloud computing, artificial intelligence, gaming, and productivity services. Its key businesses include Microsoft 365, Windows, LinkedIn, Xbox, and Azure, its cloud-computing platform. Microsoft has increasingly focused on AI, integrating AI capabilities across its products and expanding its cloud infrastructure to support growing demand and boasting a market cap of $3.9 trillion. Microsoft's stock has delivered a 10% gain year-to-date (YTD), although its 4% advance over the past year reflects a more measured longer-term performance. The stock's recent momentum has been stronger, with shares rising 8% over the past month as investors regained confidence in Microsoft's AI and cloud growth outlook. More recently, Microsoft's announcement of its Maia 300 custom AI chip, which is designed to improve computing efficiency and reduce reliance on third-party accelerators, has provided another potential catalyst as investors focus increasingly on the profitability of AI infrastructure spending. However, concerns about elevated capital expenditures, AI-related infrastructure costs, and broader volatility in technology stocks have limited MSFT stock's longer-term gains. With Microsoft reportedly considering significant cost reductions within Azure, it will be worth watching closely for evidence that Microsoft can improve cloud economics while sustaining rapid AI-driven growth. MSFT stock is currently trading at 27.46 times forward earnings and 12.07 times sales, a premium to industry peers. Microsoft reported its fiscal fourth-quarter and full-year 2026 results on July 29, delivering strong growth as Azure and AI demand continued to drive the business. For Q4 FY2026, revenue increased 18% year-over-year (YoY) to $90 billion. Operating income rose 18% to $40.6 billion, while net income jumped 31% to $35.8 billion. On a non-GAAP basis, net income increased 22% to $35.3 billion and EPS rose 23% to $4.74. The strongest growth came from the cloud business. Intelligent Cloud revenue climbed 32% to $39.3 billion, with Azure and other cloud services revenue accelerating 43% YoY. Microsoft Cloud revenue rose 27% to $59.3 billion, while commercial remaining performance obligations surged 84% to $678 billion, providing significant visibility into future cloud revenue. Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud revenue increased 14%, LinkedIn revenue rose 12%, and Dynamics 365 revenue grew 13%. In contrast, More Personal Computing revenue declined 4% to $12.9 billion. For full-year FY2026, Microsoft generated $331.8 billion in revenue, up 18%. On a non-GAAP basis, net income increased 22% to $128.8 billion and EPS rose 22% to $17.28. Additionally, the company forecasted total revenue at a midpoint of approximately $90.4 billion and projected Azure growth of 45%. Microsoft also projected about $50 billion in capital expenditures for Q1 FY2027 and roughly $175 billion for calendar 2026, underscoring that the company intends to maintain substantial AI infrastructure spending despite ongoing investor concerns over the cost and profitability of its AI buildout. Overall, the results reinforced that Azure growth is accelerating and AI adoption is expanding. However, the enormous AI-related capital spending highlights why investors are increasingly focused on whether Microsoft can convert its AI and cloud growth into sustainable margin expansion. Meanwhile, analysts remain upbeat, projecting EPS of $19.65 for fiscal 2027, up 13.7% YoY, and anticipating a further 18.3% annual increase to $23.25 in fiscal 2028. This month, UBS analyst Karl Keirstead raised MSFT stock's price target to $675 from $525, while maintaining a "Buy" rating. The upgrade reflects UBS' increased confidence in Azure and Microsoft 365 as Microsoft heads into its fiscal first-quarter results. Plus, Jefferies analyst Brent Thill raised his price target on Microsoft to $650 from $575, while maintaining a "Buy" rating. Overall, MSFT stock has a consensus "Strong Buy" rating. Of the 51 analysts covering the stock, 41 advise a "Strong Buy," four suggest a "Moderate Buy," five analysts recommend a "Hold" rating, and one offers a "Strong Sell." Volatility gripped the stock market last week amid concerns about the sustainability of the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure spending boom. The S&P 500 experienced a modest decline, but it continues to trade at a historically expensive valuation, so strong corporate earnings will be necessary to keep this bull market going. As a result, all eyes are on the current reporting season. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) will release its operating results for its fiscal 2027 first quarter (ended Sept. 30) on Oct. 28, and Wall Street will be squarely focused on the Azure cloud platform and Copilot virtual assistant, which are central to the company's AI strategy. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Microsoft stock is attractively valued heading into the report, so here's why I predict it will climb in the weeks and months that follow. AI is a powerful tool in an enterprise because it can dramatically improve productivity by automating tasks, analyzing large volumes of data, and even generating content like images and computer code. Microsoft is helping businesses tap into the power of AI through Copilot and Azure, and both represent enormous opportunities for the company. The Copilot assistant is embedded in Microsoft's legacy software products like Windows and Edge for free. But enterprises can also add it to the 365 productivity suite (which includes Word and Excel) for an additional monthly subscription fee. As of June 30, organizations worldwide were paying for 30 million Copilot licenses for 365, a staggering 50% increase from just three months earlier. However, organizations pay for more than 400 million 365 licenses for their employees, so Copilot adoption is still in the very early stages. Investors should keep an eye out for some updated numbers on Oct. 28. Then there is the Azure cloud platform, which provides every tool enterprises need to deploy AI software applications. That includes computing capacity from specialized data centers, more than 11,000 ready-made foundation models, and a platform called Foundry where they can design and manage custom AI agents. Microsoft built 88 new data centers during fiscal 2026 as part of a two-year plan to double its global infrastructure footprint. This will help Azure convert its enormous $678 billion in remaining performance obligations (RPO) into revenue, which effectively represents the platform's order backlog from customers who are waiting for more infrastructure to come online. Azure's revenue growth accelerated to 43% in the final quarter of fiscal 2026, so the platform was carrying significant momentum into the fiscal 2027 first-quarter earnings report. A further acceleration will be very bullish for Microsoft stock, but so will growth in the company's RPO, because it can be a good indicator of future revenue. Based on Microsoft's fiscal 2026 earnings of $17.95 per share, its stock is trading at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 30.1, which is a discount to its five-year average of 32. Plus, the stock has a forward P/E of 27.3 based on Wall Street's average fiscal 2027 earnings estimate of $19.78 per share (provided by Yahoo! Finance), leaving even more room for potential upside. Nevertheless, the AI industry faces increasing doubts right now that could jeopardize Microsoft's ability to actually deliver on Wall Street's fiscal 2027 earnings estimate. Labs like OpenAI and Anthropic are facing questions about their valuations and growth rates, which could reduce their ability to raise more money from investors. Moreover, neocloud companies like CoreWeave are dealing with a surge in borrowing costs on concerns they won't be able to deliver on their lofty future projections, which could weigh on the stock market overall. OpenAI has committed to spend more than $300 billion on Microsoft Azure's cloud services during the next few years, but it doesn't actually have that money today. OpenAI will have to increase its revenue significantly and also raise more money to meet all of its commitments, so if it fails on either front, Microsoft's RPO could take a hit. For all of those reasons, the first-quarter earnings report is likely to set the tone for Microsoft stock for at least the next few months. I think there could be upside ahead based on its attractive valuation, and the sheer size of its RPO –- even if we exclude OpenAI's contribution entirely, Azure is still likely to be backlogged for the next couple of years. However, investors might want to manage their risk by using a small position size given the uncertain environment. title: MSFT Stock Dips Overnight: Satya Nadella Calls Anthropic’s Fable 5 ‘Editorially Controlled’ Amid Backlash Over Safeguards - Stocktwits
content: Microsoft shares fell 1.3% in overnight trading, giving up nearly all of Thursday’s gains. MSFT stock is up 7.5% in July, in line with gains across Big Tech as investors rotate back into the sector while selling some of the year’s high-flying chip stocks. Investors are closely watching the moves as the second-quarter earnings season kicks off, with Alphabet, Tesla and Intel reporting next week. Meanwhile, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has jumped into the debate over the guardrails Anthropic has put in place for its powerful Fable 5 AI, which are also drawing criticism online for being too stringent. According to a CNBC report, Nadella reportedly told employees that Fable 5 now appears “editorially controlled” and some of the limits in the model do not “make sense.” “If you use Fable, when it refuses for any random thing, it just is like, when was the last time you had a creation tool that was so editorially controlled?” Nadella told engineers working on Microsoft’s Copilot AI software, according to a copy of his remarks that was provided to CNBC. “It doesn’t make sense.” When users ask Fable about certain topics, including elements of building large-scale AI models, Anthropic may route those queries to an older version of the model, according to Anthropic’s support page. An X user highlighted that Fable 5 directed a user to its Opus 4.8 model when asked a deeper question about cancer research. Others also reported seemingly harmless queries being redirected to the older model. Fable 5 is a scaled-down version of Anthropic’s Mythos AI model, which the company has acknowledged is highly capable of identifying vulnerabilities in technology systems and could be misused for hacking, prompting governments and enterprises to assess its risks and strengthen cybersecurity safeguards. Last month, the U.S. government directed Anthropic to restrict access to Mythos and Fable 5 for foreign users and organizations, prompting the company to temporarily withdraw both models. Anthropic later restored them after briefing officials on the safeguards it had implemented to reduce potential misuse. The development comes as Big Tech and AI firms race to put bespoke AI technology into consumers' hands. Bloomberg reported earlier this week that Anthropic will meet with investors and banks leading the offering in the coming weeks, and is looking to list its shares as soon as October. OpenAI, too, is moving forward with its IPO plans, but recent reports have said its listing could be pushed to next year. Stergiou recently said that the company would announce the 80th event and then enter an official quiet period until topline results. The acquisition is expected to close in the third quarter (Q3) of this year. ATAI stock is up more than 84% this year. UNH stock touched a 52-week high of $461.62 in Thursday’s trading session after its second-quarter (Q2) earnings results blew past Wall Street estimates. The company posted revenue of $112.03 billion, up about 0.37% from $111.62 billion in the prior-year quarter. However, it beat Wall Street expectations of $110.9 billion, as per Fiscal.ai estimates. Meanwhile, net income came in at $5.48 billion, or $6.04 per share, compared with $3.41 billion, or $3.74 per share, in the same period a year ago. The health insurer now expects 2026 adjusted earnings of $19.50 to $20 per share, up from its prior outlook of more than $18.25 per share, while maintaining its revenue guidance of more than $439 billion for the year. The company attributed the better-than-expected results and higher full-year profit outlook to improved management of elevated medical costs and greater use of AI to streamline operations.
